## 8. Models

### Sashiko (`lumenary:sashiko`, models this process)

_From: Rural Japan; when: Edo period onward; works best on: Pictures with clear light and dark areas._

Sashiko means little stabs. It began as a way for farming families to strengthen and mend cloth with white thread on indigo, and the stitch patterns became beautiful in their own right. In the simplest kind, hitomezashi, every row and column is stitched with running stitches, each starting either on the beat or half a beat off, and squares, crosses and diamonds appear from nothing.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Write r_j and c_i for the starting beat of row j and column i, each 0 or 1.
2. Draw the stitch on row j between points i and i + 1 if i + r_j is even, and the stitch on column i between j and j + 1 if j + c_i is even.
3. At any grid point exactly one of the two horizontal stitches and exactly one of the two vertical stitches meet, so the stitches join into closed loops.
4. Choose the starting beats at random, or from patterns that make diamonds, waves or steps.
5. Draw the thread thicker and brighter where the picture is light, on indigo, black or madder cloth.

**The maths:**

$$h_{i,j}=\big[(i+r_j)\bmod 2=0\big],\qquad v_{i,j}=\big[(j+c_i)\bmod 2=0\big]$$

_Whether the horizontal stitch (i, j) and the vertical stitch (i, j) are drawn. The bits r and c are random, alternating, or taken from a wave or a step pattern._ (primitives: stitch-grid, running-stitch, seeded-random)

$$h_{i-1,j}+h_{i,j}=1,\qquad v_{i,j-1}+v_{i,j}=1$$

_Each grid point has one horizontal and one vertical stitch, which is why the lines turn at every point and never meet._ (primitives: stitch-grid)

$$w=s\,\big(0.05+0.34\,\omega\,t^{1.4}\big),\qquad k=0.3+0.7\,t$$

_Thread width and brightness: s is the stitch length, ω the weight slider and t the brightness of the picture under the stitch._ (primitives: tone-mark-size, tone-curve)

**Dials:** `size` (Stitch length) = 13 [5 to 26]; `pattern` (Pattern) = "random" (random, diamonds, waves, steps); `weight` (Thread weight) = 65 [20 to 100]; `tint` (Thread colour) = "white" (white, picture, gold); `cloth` (Cloth) = "indigo" (indigo, black, madder); `seed` (New pattern) = 3.

**History:** Sashiko developed in rural Japan during the Edo period, when cotton was precious and clothes were patched and layered, especially in the north. Cloth mended for generations in this way is called boro. Hitomezashi patterns have also caught the interest of mathematicians in recent years, who have studied the loops and regions that they form.
